title: Complex arithmetic and conjugation
terms: complex number; complex field; imaginary unit; real part; imaginary part; complex conjugate; complex plane; real axis; imaginary axis; pure imaginary number.

exposition.text:
2
A complex number is z = x + iy with real x, y and i = −1. Its real and imaginary parts are x, y,
2 2
and its conjugate is z = x − iy. Conjugation preserves sums and products, and zz = x + y .
Division by a nonzero complex number is simplified by multiplying numerator and denominator
by its conjugate.
Complex numbers form a field but cannot be ordered compatibly with the ordered-field axioms:
2
a square would have to be nonnegative, contradicting i = −1. For equations involving z and
z, either write real and imaginary components or use polar form when products and powers
dominate.
The complex plane identifies x + iy with the point (x, y). The real axis consists of numbers with
y = 0; the imaginary axis consists of numbers with x = 0. Numbers of the form iy are purely
imaginary (some conventions reserve that phrase for y ̸= 0). Conjugation reflects the plane in
the real axis.

question.text:
For real a, b, consider z + z = a + ib. Which statement gives the number of complex solutions?
(A) Exactly one for every a, b.
(B) Exactly two when b = 0, and none otherwise.
(C) Infinitely many when b = 0, and none otherwise.
(D) No solutions unless a = b = 0, in which case there is one.
(E) Infinitely many for every a, b.

solution.text:
Writing z = x + iy gives 2x = a + ib. The left side is real, so b = 0 is necessary. In that
case x = a/2 and y is arbitrary, giving an entire vertical line of solutions. This real-linear
equation can be singular; complex-looking notation does not guarantee a unique solution.

How many distinct complex numbers satisfy z = z?
(A) 2 (B) 3 (C) 4 (D) 5 (E) 6

solution.text:
2
Taking moduli gives |z| = |z|, so either z = 0 or |z| = 1. In the latter case z = 1/z, and
3
the equation becomes z = 1, giving three distinct additional solutions.

question.text:
Why can the field C not be given an order satisfying the ordered-field axioms?
(A) Its addition is not commutative.
(B) It has nonzero zero divisors.
(C) Every ordered field must be finite.
2
(D) In an ordered field every nonzero square is positive, but i = −1.
(E) The conjugate of a nonreal number is not unique.

solution.text:
2
In an ordered field, 1 = 1 > 0, hence −1 < 0. Whether a nonzero element u is positive
2 2
or negative, its square is positive, since in the latter case u = (−u) . Taking u = i would
2
make −1 = i > 0, a contradiction. The ordinary complex operations otherwise satisfy the
field axioms.

question.text:
4 4
If |z| = 1 and z + z = 1, what is z + z ?
(A) 1 (B) 0 (C) −2 (D) −1 (E) 2

solution.text:
2 2 2 4 4 2
Since zz = 1, z + z = (z + z) − 2 = −1. Squaring again gives z + z = (−1) − 2 = −1.

question.text:
For real t, which point is omitted from the set {(t − i)/(t + i) : t ∈ R} on the unit circle?
(A) i (B) 1 (C) −i (D) −1 (E) No point is omitted.

solution.text:
Numerator and denominator have equal modulus, so every value lies on the unit circle.
Solving w = (t − i)/(t + i) gives t = i(1 + w)/(1 − w), which is real for every unit w ̸= 1. The
equation w = 1 would require −i = i, so that point is omitted.
